client: I've been having a really hard time since I lost my partner in a car accident six months ago. The things I used to love, like hiking or cooking new recipes, just feel completely hollow now, like I'm going through the motions without any real feeling behind it. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I guess I'm here because I don't know what else to do.
therapist: Thank you for being here, and for finding the courage to reach out even when part of you isn't sure it will help — that ambivalence makes complete sense after such a devastating loss. What you're describing, that hollowness in the things you once loved, is something many people experience in grief, and it doesn't mean those feelings of connection are gone forever. I'm wondering, when you think about your partner, is there a particular memory or moment that still feels most alive to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but I'm not sure memories are really what I need right now. When I think about him, it's like... there's this one moment where we were just sitting on the back porch watching it rain, not even talking, and it felt so complete. But bringing that up now just makes the emptiness feel bigger, not smaller, so I don't really understand how focusing on that is supposed to help.
therapist: That moment on the porch — quiet, complete, no words needed — says so much about the kind of connection you had, and it makes sense that touching it right now feels like pressing on a bruise rather than finding comfort. You're also pushing back on my suggestion, and I want you to know that's not only okay, it's actually useful — it tells us something important about what you need. Can you say a little more about what "help" might even look like for you right now, even if it's hard to imagine?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know... honestly, when I try to picture what "help" would look like, my mind just goes blank. Like, the only thing that would actually help is having him back, and that's not possible, so everything else feels kind of... pointless, I guess. I know that sounds bleak, but I don't know how to want something different when the thing I actually want is just gone.
therapist: What you're saying doesn't just sound bleak — it *is* bleak, and it's also one of the most honest things a grieving person can say, because you're right that nothing will bring him back. I notice there's something very quiet and almost resigned in the way you're sitting with that truth right now, like you've been carrying this weight for a while and you're just... tired. I don't want to rush past that — can I ask, when you say everything else feels pointless, is that a feeling that comes and goes, or does it feel more constant lately?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It's been pretty constant lately, honestly. Like, I'll have a moment here or there where I get distracted by something, but then it comes crashing back and I feel almost guilty for having forgotten, even for a second. It's like the pointlessness is just... the baseline now, and anything that feels okay is just a temporary glitch.
therapist: That guilt for having a moment of relief — like forgetting him, even briefly, is somehow a betrayal — is such a painful extra layer on top of the grief itself. Your voice carries something that sounds almost fragile right now, like you're holding a lot very carefully, and I want to make sure I'm hearing you fully. When that guilt crashes back in, what does it tell you about yourself, or about what it means to still be here living while he isn't?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It tells me I don't deserve to feel okay, like if I'm laughing or just... existing normally, then maybe he didn't matter as much as I thought he did. There's this voice that says a good friend would still be destroyed, would still be carrying it every single second. And the worst part is I can't really argue back against it, because part of me actually believes it.
therapist: That voice is lying to you, even though I understand why it feels completely convincing right now — the depth of your love for him isn't measured by how destroyed you stay, and moments of feeling okay don't erase what he meant to you. I notice you're speaking very quickly and softly, like these words are almost too heavy to say out loud, and I want to gently hold space for how much it costs you to even name this belief. What do you think *he* would say if he heard that voice telling you that you don't deserve to feel okay?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I don't know... he always used to say I was too hard on myself, that I carried guilt around like it was some kind of badge. But it feels almost wrong to use that against this voice, like I'm just finding a convenient argument to let myself off the hook. What if the voice is actually protecting me from forgetting him, and if I stop listening to it, I just... drift away from who he was to me?
therapist: He already knew this about you — that you carry guilt like a badge — and there's something quietly powerful in the fact that his voice is still in there, gently pushing back on the harsh one. What you just named is really important though: the fear that letting go of the pain means losing *him*, like the grief is the last thread connecting you. I want to sit with that for a moment — do you think it's possible to stay deeply connected to who he was to you *without* needing to punish yourself to prove it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible. But honestly, when I try to imagine just... remembering him without the weight of it, it feels almost too light, like I'd be floating away from him somehow. The guilt is heavy, but it's also familiar, and I'm not sure I know how to hold onto him without it.
therapist: The image of floating away from him is such a vivid and honest way to name what feels at stake — like the weight itself has become the relationship, the proof that he was real and that you were real together. And yet I notice something in how you're speaking right now, a kind of quickness and tension, like part of you is working very hard to hold all of this together even as you're naming it. I wonder — what if the heaviness isn't actually what keeps you close to him, but rather something you've had to build because you haven't yet found another way to carry him with you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That's... a lot to sit with, and honestly my first reaction is kind of defensive, like you're suggesting I've been doing it wrong this whole time. Because if the heaviness isn't keeping me close to him, then what have I been doing for the past two years? I don't even know what another way would look like, and that terrifies me more than the grief itself.
therapist: Your defensiveness makes complete sense, and I want to be clear — you haven't been doing anything wrong, you've been surviving an unsurvivable loss in the only way that felt possible. What strikes me is that even as you're pushing back, there's something underneath that sounds less like anger and more like exhaustion, like someone who's been holding a very heavy thing for a very long time and is just now letting themselves wonder if it has to be this heavy. The terror you're naming — not knowing what another way looks like — that's actually the first honest opening, and we don't have to rush through it or figure it out today.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know why, but something about the way you said that just... hit differently. Like I've been bracing for you to tell me I'm doing grief wrong, and instead you said I've been surviving, and I felt something kind of crack open a little in my chest. But I'm scared of that feeling too, because if I let myself actually be exhausted instead of angry, I don't know what's left to hold me together.
therapist: That cracking open you're describing — that's not you falling apart, that's something real finally getting a little air after being held so tightly for so long. And I notice something in your voice right now, something that sounds almost tender, even a little fragile, like underneath the fear there might be the tiniest bit of relief trying to surface alongside the exhaustion. I want to gently ask — what if the thing that holds you together when the anger quiets down isn't emptiness, but actually *him*, the part of him that already knew you were too hard on yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know... when you say it like that, it almost makes sense for a second, and then I feel this rush of guilt like I'm not allowed to believe it. Like if I accept that he saw something good in me, then I have to accept that I've been the one pushing that away this whole time, and that's a really uncomfortable place to sit. It's easier to just stay in the anger, honestly, because at least then I know what I'm dealing with.
therapist: The anger makes sense as a place to live — it's solid, it has edges, it tells you where you stand — but what you just described, that rush of guilt the moment something softer almost gets through, sounds exhausting in a very different way than the grief itself. There's something in your voice right now that sounds almost urgent, like you're speaking quickly to stay ahead of something that might catch up if you slow down. I'm curious — what do you think would actually happen if you let yourself sit, just for a moment, with the idea that he saw something real and good in you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
